summary: For 7–8 year olds: soil is a MIXTURE of broken-down rock particles (sand, silt, clay) plus decomposed organic matter (humus), not a single 'brown stuff'. Children investigate by hand — a settling jar separates soil into layers, a fair drainage test compares soil types, and a hand lens reveals rock grains and leaf bits. A second big idea is TIME: rock breaks down into soil very slowly. Hands-on investigation with real local soil is the core experience; cutaway diagrams, profiles and sorting tasks support vocabulary and classification.
misconceptions: 'Soil is just dirt / one single substance' — not seeing it as a mixture of rock particles and organic matter.
'Soil has nothing to do with rock' — missing that soil is broken-down rock.
'All soils are the same' — not distinguishing sandy, clay and loam by property.
'Soil forms quickly' — underestimating the very long time rock takes to break down.
'Clay soil is best because it holds water' or 'sandy is best because it drains' — treating one soil as universally superior rather than suited to different conditions.

activities.title: Settling jar: watch soil pull apart into its parts
steps: Scoop soil into a clear jar and fill with water, leaving space at the top.
Put the lid on, shake well, then set the jar down and leave it to settle.

Watch and record what settles first, what settles last, and what floats — you will typically see heavy stones and sand sink first, finer silt next, cloudy clay settle slowly on top, and dark bits of rotted leaf (humus) float; write down what you actually observe, as real soils vary.
Draw and label the layers you see, naming which are broken-down rock and which are once-living matter.
Use a hand lens on a pinch of dry soil to spot rock grains and small pieces of plant material up close.
activities.insight: Soil is a mixture: it separates into broken-down rock particles (sand/silt/clay) plus decomposed plant matter (humus), so it is not one single substance.

activities.title: Fair drainage race: sandy vs clay vs loam
steps: Set up three funnels or pots, one with sandy soil, one with clay soil, one with loam, each with the same amount of soil.
Pour the SAME amount of water into each at the same time to make it a fair test.
Watch and time how fast water drains through each, and record which is fastest and slowest.
Feel each soil (with permission) and note whether it is gritty or sticky.
Describe how the soils differ and suggest why a plant might prefer one soil over another.
activities.insight: Different soils have different, testable properties: water drains fast through sandy soil and slowly through clay, and these differences matter for which plants grow well — no single soil is universally 'best'.

activities.title: Soil profile and the slow story of soil
steps: Examine a soil-profile cutaway (organic layer on top, broken rock below, solid bedrock at the bottom) and label each layer.
For each layer, say what it is and where it came from.
Discuss or write how the solid rock below slowly breaks apart over a very long time to make the loose particles above it.
Use a lift-the-flap or 'what is soil made of?' task to recall the two main ingredients: broken rock and humus.
activities.insight: Soil forms slowly as rock gradually breaks apart over very long periods into particles that mix with decomposed living matter; in a profile like this one, the layers show that journey from solid bedrock up to soil (some soils instead form from rock pieces carried in by rivers, ice or wind).

activities.title: Sort and match soils by property
steps: Sort soil cards or samples into gritty vs sticky groups.
Match each soil type (sandy, clay, loam) to its drainage speed (fast, slow, in between).
Answer: 'What is soil made of?' choosing the answer that names both broken-down rock and decomposed organic matter.
For plants: discuss why a soil's drainage might help or hinder certain plants.
activities.insight: Children can classify soils by observable properties and articulate that soil's two core ingredients are broken rock and humus.

checkQuestion: Where does soil come from — has it always just been there, or is it made from something? And what is soil actually made of?
checkAnswer: Soil is made over a very long time as rock gradually breaks down into tiny particles, mixed with decomposed plant and animal matter (humus). So soil comes partly from broken-down rock and partly from once-living things — it didn't just appear.
